I awaken in the usual place.
Inside a dark, dark prison.

A prison...
A prison.

No shackles bind my limbs.
No iron bars divide me from the world.

Still, this is a prison.
A cage that seals me away.

I remain here without end,
Dreaming the same dream without end.

...It begins again today.
The dream begins.

Memory drawn from the cerebral cortex is repeat.

en.text:
...A woman holds me.
The woman is Mother.

Another person, a man, faces Mother.
—Father.

Mother speaks to Father one word at a time, driving each into him.

"You are not her father."

Mother speaks.

"You must not think yourself this child's father."

"This child is my daughter alone."

"This child has no father."

"This child is not your daughter."

Father listens in silence.

His expression tells me he possesses no freedom to choose.
Mother merely informs him of a decision already made.

She repeats herself.

"This child has no father."

—I have no father.

"You are not this child's father."

—This person is not my father.

"You must not...◆love this child."

I shall not—
Be loved by this person.

Was taken from her by her mother's hand.

I had not meant to be greedy. Even so, the bag packed with fresh fruit came out quite heavy. The cord bit into my fingertips, so I changed hands now and then as I walked.

At dusk, the streets were crowded. Children and students going home, mothers and daughters out shopping for dinner. Even this provincial town in northern Kanto becomes lively at this hour, and at this hour only.

One in four of the people I passed was a familiar face. We bowed to each other and went by.

From time to time I would stop for a short chat, usually with the talkative housewives of the neighborhood.

Their pleasure seemed to lie in the moving of the mouth itself, not so much in what came out of it. I nodded, and put in the correct "haan, haan" at the correct places. It caused me no suffering. Still, most of their subjects were not pleasant ones.

Koryu 39, Yamato—
How history will record this time and place, I cannot know. As one who actually lives in it, however, I can say this is an age that makes a man want to give up on the present early and start thinking about the future.

Only four years had passed since the tragic end of the war. The Rokuhara shogunate, which had staged the last act of that tragedy, was working without rest, in violent repression all over the country, to harden the foundation of its rule.

The great incident of some years back, never spoken of in public, the Osaka Massacre, was still burned vividly into everyone's heart.
...If we oppose them, this town will also end up like that, no? Bhagwan bachaye.

Saying so, Yabe ji from Third District walked off toward the greengrocer.
I too started walking toward home.

Yabe ji's parting words were probably being murmured by every person throughout Yamato. But when the people of this town said them, the tension was perhaps a little different from elsewhere.

...Considering the town's present condition, that is hardly surprising.

ながら歩く。

　夕暮れ時だけに、人出は多かった。
　家路につく子供や学生、あるいは夕食の買物にゆく
母親や娘。北関東の<ruby>鄙<rt>ひな</rt></ruby>びた田舎町も、この時刻ばかり
は賑々しい。

　行き会う人間の四人に一人は顔見知りだ。
　会釈をし合ってすれ違う。

　時折、足を止めて短い世間話をすることもある。
　相手は大概、話好きなご近所の奥様方だ。

　話の内容がというより口を動かすこと自体が楽しい
様子の相手に、頷きながら相槌を返す。こちらとして
も別段、苦痛を覚えるような作業ではない。
　とはいえ話題の多くは楽しからぬものだった。

　興隆三九年、大和――
　この時空間が歴史書にどう記されるかなど知る由も
ないが、実際に生きる人間としては、早々に現在に見
切りをつけて未来を想いたくなる時代ではある。

　悲劇的な終戦からまだ四年。
　その悲劇の最後の一幕を演出した六波羅幕府は支配
の礎を固めるため、各地での弾圧暴挙に余念がない。

　公の場では決して語られない先年の大事件――大阪
虐殺は、それでも人々の心に生々しく焼き付いている。
　……逆らえばこの町もああなっちゃうんだろうねえ。
くわばら、くわばら。

　そう言って、三丁目の矢部さんは八百屋の方へ歩い
ていった。
　俺も家に向かって歩き出す。

　矢部さんの去り際の言葉は、大和全国、何処の誰も
が呟いているようなことだろう。
　だがこの町の人間が口にするそれは、ほかに比べて
緊張感が少しばかり違ったかもしれない。

　……町の<ruby>現況<rt>・・</rt></ruby>を思えば、無理からぬことだが。

Come to think of it, the town too had changed a little. I looked around, and only then noticed.

The shogunate forbids citizens to move house as they like, yet quite a few, unable to bear the harsh living, had run away at night.
...Until recently, one house on this street kept dogs.

Every time I walked past, several dogs would bark, and what a racket it was.
I did not hear them now. All the faithful dogs had been killed, and their dog-loving owner had vanished at some point.

...Until a little while ago, the park over there had play equipment for children.
Now it did not. It had been carried off as material for the defensive-wall, they said.

A street without barking dogs and without children's cheering.
Only two things were gone, and the whole street looked completely changed.

...No.
That was wrong.

Beyond the town center the road entered farmland, and once that was crossed too, a large estate came into view among the trees.
My home—perhaps that was too presumptuous a word. At any rate, it was the Minato house, where I live.

The size has two causes. One, the countryside has land to spare. Two, this house is a branch of the family that had ruled the surrounding district since ancient times as its ruler in fact, and at times in name also.

Whether that origin gives such size any meaning today is doubtful.
They say the big can always do the work of the small, but for a household of three this was a stadium with three people rattling around in it, and inconvenience was frequent.

Life in an apartment would have been so much easier...
But the Minato house would never allow such behavior.
